topic: Day 1 · Glucose Physiology & the Pathophysiology of Diabetic Emergencies
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Diabetes & Endocrine Unit
speakerBio: An endocrinologist who teaches diabetic emergencies from the biochemistry outward, insisting that a registrar who can draw the vicious cycle on a napkin never mismanages a DKA. Her refrain: treat the switch, not the sugar.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — 02:40, resus bay 1

A 19-year-old student is brought in by her flatmate. She has been vomiting since yesterday, is breathing deeply and fast — a strange, sighing pattern — and there is a sweet, nail-varnish smell on her breath. She is drowsy, her lips are cracked, her eyes are sunken. Heart rate 124, BP 98/60, respiratory rate 32. The capillary glucose meter reads "HI". The nurse hands you a gas and asks what to do. Stop. Before a single millilitre of fluid or unit of insulin, understand this: everything you are about to see — the breathing, the smell, the drowsiness, the shock — flows from one broken switch. There is no insulin in this body. Get the mechanism and the whole week writes itself.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole conference

Diabetic ketoacidosis is not a sugar problem. It is an insulin-deficiency problem — the hyperglycaemia is a symptom, the ketoacidosis is the disease, and you treat the fuel switch, not the glucose number.

If you take one idea from this entire conference, take this: the danger in front of you is driven by absent insulin action, not by a high blood sugar. The glucose is the loudest sign but the least lethal one. The lethal process is the body tearing itself apart for fuel because it believes it is starving — even while it drowns in glucose it cannot use. This session builds the machine from first principles so that every decision in Sessions 2, 3 and 4 (diagnose → resuscitate → clear the ketones) becomes obvious.

2 · Insulin — the master storage hormone ⚙️

Insulin is the body's single most important anabolic, fuel-storage signal. It is the hormone of the fed state. When it is present, it tells every tissue the same thing: "Fuel is plentiful — store it, build, stop breaking things down." Concretely, insulin:

  • Drives glucose into cells — recruits GLUT4 transporters in muscle and fat, lowering blood glucose.
  • Suppresses hepatic glucose output — switches off gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver.
  • Suppresses lipolysis — this is the single most important action in DKA. Insulin restrains hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, keeping free fatty acids locked in the fat cell.
  • Promotes protein synthesis and drives potassium into cells alongside glucose.

The counterweight to insulin is a quartet of counter-regulatory (catabolic) hormones — glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol and growth hormone. In health, insulin and glucagon sit on a see-saw, and insulin wins in the fed state. Remove insulin, and the see-saw slams the other way with nothing to oppose it.

HormoneDirectionWhat it does in the fasting/stress state
InsulinAnabolic (storage)Glucose uptake, stops lipolysis, stops ketogenesis, stops hepatic glucose output. The brake on the whole system.
GlucagonCatabolicThe prime mover in DKA. Drives gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and — critically — switches the liver into ketone-production mode.
Catecholamines (adrenaline)CatabolicStimulate lipolysis and glycogenolysis, further suppress the little insulin that remains. Poured out by the stress/dehydration.
CortisolCatabolicPromotes gluconeogenesis, proteolysis and insulin resistance. Sustains the crisis.
Growth hormoneCatabolicAdds insulin resistance and lipolysis.
💡 Pearl — the bimolecular switch

DKA is best understood as an insulin-to-glucagon ratio problem. It is not just that insulin is low; it is that the ratio of insulin to glucagon collapses. A low ratio flips the liver from a glucose-storing, fat-storing organ into a glucose-exporting, ketone-producing factory. Give exogenous insulin and you restore the ratio — that is precisely why insulin, not fluid, is what finally shuts off the ketogenesis.

3 · The insulin-deficient state — following the vicious cycle 🔄

Now remove insulin (or let it become ineffective) and trace what happens, step by step. This is the spine of the whole conference — draw it out until it is automatic.

  1. No insulin action. Glucose cannot enter insulin-dependent tissues (muscle, fat). The cells are metabolically starving in a sea of glucose.
  2. Unopposed counter-regulation. With no insulin brake, glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol and GH run wild — the body reads starvation even amid hyperglycaemia.
  3. Hepatic glucose output soars. Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis flood the blood with glucose that nothing can take up → hyperglycaemia climbs.
  4. Unrestrained lipolysis. Hormone-sensitive lipase, no longer restrained by insulin, breaks adipose triglyceride into free fatty acids (FFAs), which pour into the portal circulation.
  5. Hepatic ketogenesis. The high-glucagon liver shuttles FFAs into mitochondria (glucagon lowers malonyl-CoA, disinhibiting carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1, the gate to beta-oxidation). FFAs are beta-oxidised to acetyl-CoA faster than the Krebs cycle can use it → acetyl-CoA is diverted to ketone bodies.
  6. Ketoacidosis. The dominant ketone is beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), then acetoacetate, and a little acetone (the breath smell). These are strong organic acids — they dissociate, dumping H⁺ and consuming bicarbonate → a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
  7. Osmotic diuresis. Once blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (~10 mmol/L / 180 mg/dL) glucose spills into urine, dragging water and electrolytes with it → polyuria, dehydration, and profound total-body loss of potassium, sodium, phosphate and magnesium.
  8. The dehydration spiral. Fluid loss → falling circulating volume → falling renal perfusion → falling GFR → the kidney can no longer excrete glucose or ketones → glucose and ketones climb faster → osmotic diuresis worsens the volume loss. The vicious cycle closes and accelerates.
No insulin → the body eats its own fat → the liver turns that fat into acid → the acid and the sugar together pull water out through the kidney → dehydration shuts the kidney down → everything gets worse. One broken switch, one accelerating spiral.
🎯 Why beta-hydroxybutyrate, not acetoacetate, dominates

In the ketogenic liver the redox state is highly reduced (a high NADH:NAD⁺ ratio from furious beta-oxidation). That equilibrium pushes acetoacetate → beta-hydroxybutyrate, so BHB typically outnumbers acetoacetate ~3:1 (and much more in severe/hypoperfused DKA). This matters clinically in two ways: (1) measure BHB directly (capillary ketone meters read BHB) — it is the true marker of the acidosis; (2) the old urine nitroprusside dipstick detects acetoacetate only, so it under-reads at the sickest moment and can paradoxically appear to rise during treatment as BHB converts back to acetoacetate. The improving patient's urine ketones can look worse — do not be fooled.

4 · The osmotic diuresis — where the water and electrolytes go 💧

The dehydration of a hyperglycaemic crisis is not incidental; it is central, and it is enormous. Understand the plumbing:

  • Glucose is freely filtered at the glomerulus and normally fully reabsorbed. Above the renal threshold, reabsorption is saturated and glucose remains in the tubular fluid.
  • That glucose is an osmotic agent — it holds water in the tubule, producing a brisk diuresis and dragging sodium, potassium, magnesium and phosphate out with it.
  • Typical deficits by the time DKA is established: water ~100 mL/kg (5–7 L), sodium 7–10 mmol/kg, potassium 3–5 mmol/kg — even when the serum potassium looks normal or high.
⚠️ Danger — the potassium that lies

Total-body potassium is massively depleted in DKA, yet the serum potassium on arrival is often normal or high. Two reasons: (1) acidosis drives K⁺ out of cells in exchange for H⁺; (2) the lack of insulin removes the signal that normally pushes K⁺ into cells. The moment you give insulin and correct the acidosis, potassium floods back into cells and the serum level can plummet, risking fatal arrhythmia. This is the physiological reason behind one of the hardest rules in medicine: never start insulin in DKA until you know the potassium and it is above 3.5 mmol/L (Session 4). The whole treatment is built on a fact from this mechanism session.

5 · DKA vs HHS — same spectrum, one decisive difference 🔀

DKA and the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) are two ends of one spectrum of insulin deficiency. The single variable that separates them is how much insulin action remains — specifically, whether there is enough insulin to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis.

FeatureDKAHHS
Typical patientType 1 (or ketosis-prone type 2)Older type 2, often with a precipitant (infection, MI)
Insulin stateAbsolute deficiency — essentially noneRelative deficiency — a residual amount persists
The key consequenceNot enough insulin to stop lipolysis → ketogenesis proceeds → acidosisEnough residual insulin to suppress lipolysis/ketogenesis, but not enough to control glucose
Ketones/acidosisMarked ketosis, high-anion-gap acidosis (pH <7.3)Minimal ketosis, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15
GlucoseHigh (often >11–30 mmol/L)Extreme (often >30–40 mmol/L / >600 mg/dL)
OsmolalityRaisedExtreme — >320 mOsm/kg; the dominant threat
Onset / dehydrationHours–1 day; very dehydratedDays–weeks; even more profoundly dehydrated (deficit ~100–220 mL/kg)
Dominant dangerThe acidosisThe hyperosmolality (thrombosis, obtundation, coma)
💡 Pearl — the one-line discriminator

DKA is a problem of acid; HHS is a problem of osmolality. The reason HHS has little ketosis is beautifully simple: the small amount of insulin still present is too weak to move glucose but strong enough to keep the fat cell shut. Suppress lipolysis and you suppress ketogenesis — no fatty-acid substrate, no ketones, no acidosis. The trade-off is that the glucose climbs unopposed for days, osmolality soars, and the patient desiccates. Same broken switch, dialled to a different setting.

🎯 The overlap zone — mixed DKA/HHS

Roughly a third of hyperglycaemic emergencies are mixed: ketoacidosis and hyperosmolality together. These patients are the sickest and carry the highest mortality. The 2024 ADA/EASD consensus on hyperglycaemic crises stresses treating both processes and not forcing a patient into one box. Recognise the overlap on the mechanism — insulin deficiency is a dial, not a switch.

6 · Why the glucose is the least of your worries 🧠

New clinicians instinctively fixate on the "HI" reading. But consider: a patient can be in life-threatening DKA with a glucose of only 10–12 mmol/L (euglycaemic DKA — Session 2), and a patient in HHS with a glucose of 45 mmol/L may not be acidotic at all. The glucose number correlates poorly with how close the patient is to dying. What kills is:

  • The acidosis (myocardial depression, arrhythmia, obtundation, eventually respiratory fatigue when Kussmaul breathing can no longer compensate).
  • The volume depletion (shock, acute kidney injury, the closing vicious cycle).
  • The electrolyte shifts — above all potassium — during treatment.
  • In HHS, hyperosmolality and its thrombotic and neurological consequences.
You are not treating a number on a glucometer. You are refilling a tank, switching off an acid factory, and guarding a potassium. The glucose comes down almost as a side-effect.

7 · Kussmaul, the breath, and the compensations 🌬️

The deep sighing hyperventilation (Kussmaul respiration) is the lungs blowing off CO₂ to generate a compensatory respiratory alkalosis that partially offsets the metabolic acidosis — a textbook example of the body defending pH. The fruity/acetone breath is exhaled acetone. Recognise both as signs of a severe acidosis the body is straining to compensate; when a tiring patient's respiratory rate falls and their pCO₂ rises, that is exhaustion and impending decompensation, not improvement.

☠️ M&M — "The sugar was only fifteen"

A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes attended his GP feeling unwell with vomiting and abdominal pain two days after a viral illness; he had been eating little and had reduced his insulin because he "wasn't eating." His capillary glucose was 15.4 mmol/L — high but "not that high" — so he was reassured, given oral rehydration advice and sent home. He was found collapsed the next morning and arrested in the ambulance; his arrival pH was 6.86 with a BHB of 7.2 mmol/L. The lesson runs straight from this session's mechanism: DKA is driven by insulin deficiency and ketogenesis, not by the height of the glucose. Reducing basal insulin during illness ("sick-day" error) removed the last brake on lipolysis; the modest glucose reflected poor intake, not safety. Anyone who anchored on the sugar missed a full-blown ketoacidosis. Check ketones, not just glucose, in any unwell person with diabetes — and never stop basal insulin.

8 · Take-home 🎯

  • DKA is an insulin-deficiency disease, not a glucose disease. The ketoacidosis is the illness; the hyperglycaemia is a symptom.
  • The engine is the collapsed insulin:glucagon ratio → unrestrained lipolysis → hepatic ketogenesis → beta-hydroxybutyrate-dominant high-anion-gap acidosis.
  • Hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → water and electrolyte loss → falling GFR → worse hyperglycaemia: a closing, accelerating vicious cycle.
  • DKA (absolute deficiency, type 1) vs HHS (relative deficiency, type 2): enough residual insulin in HHS to suppress ketogenesis but not glucose → extreme hyperosmolality instead of acidosis.
  • Serum potassium lies — total-body K⁺ is depleted; insulin will drop it. This one fact underwrites the whole treatment.
  • Measure BHB directly; the urine nitroprusside test reads acetoacetate only and can mislead.

Next session: turning this mechanism into a bedside diagnosis — the triad, how to grade severity with the JBDS markers, and the trap that will fool you if you trust the glucose: euglycaemic DKA.

moderatorQs.q: A patient arrives in florid DKA with a serum potassium of 5.4 mmol/L. Why is it dangerous to read that as 'the potassium is fine', and how does the mechanism dictate your first move?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the serum potassium in DKA badly misrepresents total-body potassium, which is profoundly depleted (3–5 mmol/kg lost through the osmotic diuresis). The serum level is falsely reassuring for two mechanistic reasons: the acidosis drives K⁺ out of cells in exchange for H⁺, and the absence of insulin removes the normal signal pushing K⁺ into cells. The instant you give insulin and correct the acidosis, potassium is driven back intracellularly and the serum level can fall precipitously into a range that causes fatal arrhythmia. So the mechanism dictates the rule: establish the potassium before insulin, ensure it is above 3.5 mmol/L, and add potassium replacement to the fluids (typically once K⁺ is below ~5.5 with urine output) so that as insulin acts you are refilling the cell, not emptying the serum.

moderatorQs.q: Two patients have identical insulin deficiency as the root cause, yet one develops DKA with pH 7.05 and the other HHS with pH 7.34 and glucose 48 mmol/L. What single physiological variable best explains the divergence?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The decisive variable is the amount of residual insulin action, and specifically whether it is sufficient to suppress lipolysis. In DKA (usually type 1) the deficiency is absolute: with no insulin to restrain hormone-sensitive lipase, free fatty acids pour to the liver, are beta-oxidised, and are converted to ketoacids → high-anion-gap acidosis. In HHS (usually type 2) the deficiency is relative: a small amount of insulin persists — too little to move glucose into cells (so glucose climbs to extreme levels over days) but enough to keep the fat cell shut, so lipolysis and therefore ketogenesis are suppressed and there is little acidosis. No fatty-acid substrate, no ketones. The price HHS pays for avoiding acidosis is unopposed hyperglycaemia and extreme hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), which becomes the dominant lethal threat.

moderatorQs.q: Why does capillary beta-hydroxybutyrate track the severity of DKA better than a urine ketone dipstick, and why can urine ketones appear to worsen as the patient improves?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is the dominant ketone in DKA — the highly reduced redox state of the ketogenic liver (high NADH:NAD⁺) pushes the acetoacetate ⇌ BHB equilibrium toward BHB, often 3:1 or more, and worse when tissues are hypoperfused. Capillary meters measure BHB directly, so they quantify the true acid load in real time. The urine nitroprusside dipstick detects acetoacetate only (not BHB), so at the sickest moment it under-reads. As treatment restores perfusion and the redox state normalises, BHB is converted back to acetoacetate — so the urine dipstick can rise even as the patient is genuinely recovering. This is exactly why modern JBDS guidance monitors capillary BHB (and the venous bicarbonate/pH), not urine ketones, to track resolution.

audienceQs.q: I understand the glucose is high because insulin is missing, but where does the acid actually come from? Why does a lack of insulin make someone acidotic?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The acid comes from fat, processed by the liver. Insulin's most important job in this context is to keep fat locked inside adipose cells by restraining hormone-sensitive lipase. Remove insulin and, with glucagon and adrenaline unopposed, that lipase runs free: triglyceride is broken into free fatty acids that flood to the liver. The high-glucagon liver drives those fatty acids into mitochondria and beta-oxidises them to acetyl-CoA far faster than the Krebs cycle can burn it, so the surplus is diverted into ketone bodies — mainly beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. These are organic acids: they dissociate, release H⁺, and consume bicarbonate, producing a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. So the sequence is: no insulin → fat breakdown → hepatic ketone production → acid. The high glucose and the acid are two separate consequences of the same missing hormone.

audienceQs.q: The patient is clearly dehydrated but they've been drinking loads of water and passing loads of urine. If they're drinking, why are they so dry?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because the problem is an obligatory osmotic diuresis the kidney cannot switch off, and no amount of oral water keeps up with it. Once blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (~10 mmol/L), glucose spills into the urine and acts as an osmotic agent, holding water in the tubule and dragging it — plus sodium, potassium, magnesium and phosphate — out of the body. The polydipsia (huge thirst and drinking) is the body trying and failing to compensate for litres of ongoing loss. As dehydration worsens, the circulating volume falls, renal perfusion and GFR drop, the kidney can no longer clear glucose or ketones, and both climb faster — worsening the diuresis further. That is the vicious cycle. By the time DKA is established the water deficit is typically ~100 mL/kg (5–7 L), which is why fluid resuscitation, not just insulin, is a pillar of treatment.

audienceQs.q: Why is the breathing so deep and fast, and should I be worried if it suddenly slows down and the patient looks calmer?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The deep, sighing hyperventilation is Kussmaul respiration — the lungs deliberately blowing off carbon dioxide to create a compensatory respiratory alkalosis that partly offsets the metabolic acidosis and defends the blood pH. It is a sign the body is working hard against a severe acid load, and the fruity smell is exhaled acetone. And yes — be very worried if it slows and the patient looks 'calmer'. A falling respiratory rate with a rising CO₂ in an acidotic patient is usually exhaustion, not recovery: the respiratory muscles are tiring and compensation is failing, which precedes decompensation, obtundation and arrest. Treat a suddenly 'settled', drowsy DKA patient as a deteriorating one until the gas proves otherwise, and escalate immediately.
